hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer When I Work from a written spec. Claude passed all twenty checks, and found eighty-four gaps in my spec.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of When I Work a single location actually uses. A weekly schedule, built in draft and published as a whole. Open shifts that staff claim. Swaps and drops that a manager approves. And labor cost before you publish.

The core rule is the conflict check. Every time a shift is assigned, it's checked. Overlaps, approved time off, a missing position or an inactive person are refused outright. Being unavailable, less than ten hours of rest, or going over weekly hours are warnings. A manager can save anyway, but only with a note. Staff can't override anything.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. People, positions and time off. Building and publishing the week. My shifts, claims, swaps and drops. Then the calendar feed, export and print. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser.

Here's what it built. The schedule for the week of October nineteenth, with an open Saturday barista shift, costed at one hundred and forty-four dollars. Moving Tuesday's opening shift to Jo brings up a warning. Jo is unavailable on Tuesdays. Publishing the week emails each of the eight people their shifts. Lee and Ana both claim the open Saturday shift, first and second in line. The print view shows hours, never wages. And on a phone, Lee can accept Jo's swap.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all twenty checks passed, along with sixty-six automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The test build exposed eighty-four places where Claude had to guess. An approved swap would have sent two emails for one change. A shift a manager opened after publishing reached nobody. And the printed schedule, posted where staff can see it, showed labor cost. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test production sign-in, real email delivery, a hosted scheduler, or real calendar apps. The feed was fetched by its link, not subscribed to from a phone.

So is it worth building? When I Work costs two dollars fifty per user per month for one location, and five dollars for several. For a cafe with twenty staff, that's six hundred dollars a year. It's cheap, so the case for building is fit, not price. If you want a time clock, payroll integrations or several locations, buy it. If your schedule lives in a spreadsheet and changes happen by text, build it.
Everything is in one file. The data model, nine rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all twenty checks, with the eighty-four fixes already in.
